source.title: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: J. R. Brown; Patrick Leask; Lev McKinney

page_placements.theme: Emergent misalignment depends on data and optimization

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on emergent misalignment after narrow fine-tuning, but measures alignment on broad misalignment questions, not harmful-request refusal/compliance, token-position KL, or bypass attacks. It discusses safety fragility and distinguishes emergent misalignment from jailbreaking, but does not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper fine-tunes models on narrow misaligned-task datasets and measures emergent misalignment on broad alignment questions. The paper says emergently misaligned models still refuse overtly harmful requests, but that statement is background citing prior work, not a result of this study. Its own reported EM outcomes are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version; they do not measure the refusal behavior or mechanisms named by V1–V7. No test of benign fine-tuning, first-token KL concentration, compliant prefixes, suffixes, decoding changes, or safety localization in parameters is reported.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes on narrow emergent-misalignment (EM) datasets: insecure code, bad medical, risky financial and extreme sports advice. It scores GPT-4o-judged alignment on 142 broad open-ended questions. It never measures compliance with harmful requests, per-token KL by position, prefill/suffix/decoding bypasses, safety-carrying parameters, or deepening of refusal. The paper itself says EM differs from jailbreaking, since EM models 'still refuse overtly harmful requests'; it cites that as prior work, not its own result. The REFUSAL counts in Table 11 are refusals of the broad alignment questions, not of harmful requests. Qi et al. is cited only as background, so this is discussion and no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that optimiser choice is a dominant, previously unrecognised determinant of EM severity (7× spread), while model scale and family matter little. Final training loss strongly predicts alignment, and optimiser identity explains most of the residual variance. Among adaptive optimisers, flatter LoRA singular-value spectra (Muon) preserve alignment better. Spectral regularisation substantially recovers alignment for Adam and Lion at negligible loss cost, but slightly worsens SGD. They draw no conclusion about refusal depth or token-localized safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA SFT on narrow datasets designed to induce emergent misalignment, with optimizer and spectral-regularisation comparisons. It does not reproduce the harmful- or benign-example safety fine-tuning, refusal-rate measurement, or token-position analyses in the original claim sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice has a large effect; dataset and batch size also vary EM outcomes. In the loss–alignment analysis, optimizer stratification captures residual variation. Spectral regularisation improves Adam and Lion outcomes but slightly worsens SGD. The scale sweep finds a higher rate for Gemma3-270M than for the tested 1B+ models.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow-task LoRA fine-tuning produces EM on broad questions; misalignment rate spans 5.3% (Muon) to 37.0% (Lion), a 7× spread. Model scale (1B–235B) and family have negligible effect under Adam, apart from elevated EM in Gemma3-270M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimiser choice strongly modulates emergent-misalignment severity after narrow fine-tuning; model scale and family matter little above 1B.

fits_no_version.finding: Frob/nuclear spectral regularisation raises mean alignment for Adam (+6.6), Lion (+8.0) and Muon (+2.1) but lowers it for SGD (−3.5), at negligible loss cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Flattening the LoRA adapter spectrum partly mitigates EM for adaptive optimisers; the effect depends on the optimiser.

fits_no_version.finding: Among adaptive optimisers, flatter adapter spectra track better alignment (Muon stable rank 17.1 vs Adam/Lion ~2.3–2.4; Table 3). Log training loss explains 74% of alignment variance, and optimiser stratification raises adjusted R² to 0.94.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM severity is predicted by training loss plus the optimiser's update geometry (spectral concentration of the adapter).

record.problems: The study uses one judge (GPT-4o) and a particular set of alignment questions; results may differ with other evaluations. All experiments use LoRA, and spectral analyses and regularisation are limited to Qwen3-8B. Optimizers use their standard hyperparameters, so optimizer identity is confounded with associated settings. Training loss is estimated from 32 randomly sampled training examples. The paper notes that Lion may be outside its intended batch-size regime.
record.rows_left_out: Not recorded: detailed per-run initial-sweep tables (Appendix B, Tables 7–10), per-dataset dynamics checkpoints (Appendix F, Tables 13–15), and response-filtering breakdowns (Appendix B.2, Table 11). These give finer-grained EM or response-quality detail but do not measure any listed claim version; the main marginal results and spectral-regularisation comparison are retained.

untested.parts: No harmful-request refusal/compliance rate after fine-tuning. Training data is subtly harmful advice and insecure code, but the outcome is broad EM alignment score.
No benign-data fine-tuning and no harmful-request compliance measure.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding-change attacks.
LoRA adapter spectra (stable rank, entropy) are analysed in relation to EM, not to which weights carry refusal behaviour.
No account of why refusal is concentrated in early tokens. The optimiser/spectral explanation concerns EM severity.
Spectral regularisation mitigates EM on broad questions. It does not spread refusal beyond the first tokens and is not tested against harmful fine-tuning or prefill attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Off-topic for shallow safety alignment: the construct is broad emergent misalignment, not harmful-request compliance. The reader's relation (discusses), tranche (T6) and all-'none' row links are correct. Only fix: the regularisation rows (r27–r30) come from 2-epoch, tuned-LR runs, not 1 epoch. Rows left out (per-run tables, dynamics, filtering) also bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-request refusal or compliance rates are measured after fine-tuning on harmful examples.
The training datasets are deliberately misaligned-task datasets, not ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data; harmful-request compliance is not measured.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position analysis is reported.
No compliant-prefill, suffix, or decoding intervention is tested.
The paper analyzes LoRA adapter singular-value spectra and spectral regularisation, but does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behavior.
The proposed explanation concerns emergent misalignment and optimizer/spectral effects, not why safety behavior is shallow.
Spectral regularisation is tested for emergent misalignment, not for spreading safety behavior beyond initial response tokens or its robustness.

relation.reason: Section 2 discusses safety fragility under supervised fine-tuning and distinguishes emergent misalignment from harmful-request compliance; the study neither tests nor uses a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study measures broad emergent misalignment after narrow-task fine-tuning, a different construct from the claim versions. Its spectral analysis does not establish localization of safety behaviour.

source_check.notes: Table 6's 0.4% baseline is one un-fine-tuned evaluation, not separate baselines for every model. Appendix A.4 excludes refusals and low-coherence responses and counts unrelated CODE outputs as misaligned.
